name: CapWords
tagline: Auto-generated animated captions and subtitles for short-form video.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The pipeline underneath this is genuinely commoditized: Whisper gives you word-level timestamps, ffmpeg burns styled subtitles, and an agent can wire both together in an afternoon. What you will not get in one session is the part people actually pay for, which is a caption style that looks like the ones going viral this month, applied without you touching a config file. Word-by-word pop, keyword highlighting, emoji injection, safe-area placement for each platform: each is easy alone and tedious as a set. If you edit on a phone, the DIY version is dead on arrival because it is a desktop script. If you edit on a laptop and only need two or three looks you keep reusing, the script wins on cost and speed.
coreLoopDIY: Transcribes a video locally with word-level timestamps, then renders styled karaoke-style burned-in captions with ffmpeg.
requirements: faster-whisper model download (a few GB on first run)
a machine with enough CPU or a GPU, unless you enjoy waiting
fonts you actually have licensed for the styles you want
whatYouLose: Preset caption styles that already look current, instead of the two you hand-tune
Any mobile or in-browser editing; this is a terminal script on your laptop
A visual timeline for fixing the one word Whisper mangled in a proper noun
Fast iteration: every style tweak means a full re-render
Speaker detection, auto-reframing, filler-word cuts and the rest of the adjacent feature creep
moatNotes: Transcription is a free model. Taste in caption design, and shipping it as one button on a phone, is the product.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because captions are a volume job. If you post daily, the difference between a fifteen second export on a phone and a two minute terminal render plus a style argument you half remember is the difference between shipping and not. Paid caption tools also absorb the boring maintenance: new platform aspect ratios, new fonts, new trends in how text pops, transcription quality on noisy audio. A local script solves the technical problem completely and the workflow problem partly.
notes: The transcription is free, the taste is not, and taste is what you are buying.
prompt:
Build a local command line tool called "capgen" that burns animated captions into short-form videos. No accounts, no cloud APIs, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Python 3.11, single package plus a Typer CLI entry point
- faster-whisper for transcription with word_timestamps=True
- ffmpeg via subprocess for rendering
- ASS (Advanced SubStation Alpha) subtitles for styling, generated by hand as text, no subtitle library
- uv for dependency management, pyproject.toml, no requirements.txt

Command:
  capgen render INPUT.mp4 --style bold-pop --out OUTPUT.mp4

Behavior:
1. Extract audio to 16kHz mono wav in a temp dir.
2. Transcribe with faster-whisper (default model "small", overridable with --model). Cache the raw word-level JSON next to the input as INPUT.words.json and reuse it if it exists unless --retranscribe is passed.
3. Group words into caption chunks: max 3 words or 1.2 seconds per chunk, break on sentence punctuation.
4. Generate an .ass file where the active word in each chunk is highlighted using inline color and scale overrides, so playback reads as word-by-word pop.
5. Burn in with ffmpeg: -vf "ass=captions.ass", copy audio, h264 yuv420p, faststop for web.

Styles: ship exactly two, defined in a styles.toml file: "bold-pop" (heavy sans, white text, black outline, yellow active word) and "clean-lower" (medium sans, no outline, subtle drop shadow, no color change). Font family, size, outline width, active color, vertical position as percentage of frame height, and max chunk length all come from that file. Do not build a style editor.

Also add: capgen edit INPUT.words.json which opens the transcript as an editable plain text file so misheard words can be fixed before rendering, keeping timings intact.

Out of scope, do not build: a GUI, a web app, emoji insertion, speaker diarization, auto-reframing, translation, batch queues.

Deliverables: working code, a README with install steps and a real example command, and one sample styles.toml. Fail loudly with a clear message if ffmpeg is missing.
